**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.
In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)
Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.
At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)
Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.
The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.

#### Sports Achievements
In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major marathon in New York and won. She was the first African woman to win the New York Marathon. As a consequence, she became an important sporting role model. Kenya, at last, had a female runner to rank alongside its talented male athletes.
After this initial success, Tegla Loroupe went on to win many major marathons around the world. Between 1997 and 1999, she won three consecutive world half marathon Championships. In the World Championships, she won bronze in the 10,000m in both 1995 and 1999. Between 19 April 1998 – 30 September 2001, Loroupe held the world record for the marathon. She initially set a time of 2:20:47 in the 1998 Rotterdam marathon. In 1999, she broke her own record, setting a time of 2:20:43 in the Berlin marathon. She has also held world records at one hour, 20, 25 and 30 kilometres.
The marathon proved to be Loroupe’s most successful distance. She won the marathons of Rotterdam three times between 1997 and 1999, New York in 1994 and 1995, Berlin in 1999, London and Rome in 2000 and Lausanne in 2002. Loroupe holds the world records for 20, 25 and 30 kilometres and previously held the world marathon record. She is the three-time World Half-Marathon champion. She has won marathons in London, Boston, Rotterdam, Hong Kong, Berlin, Rome and many other cities.
In 2003, Loroupe founded the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation and has been an active advocate for peace. She has been successful in bringing members of warring tribes together in conflict areas in East Africa.

#### Sports Achievements
In 2006, she founded the 10km Peace Race, which included 2,000 warriors from six different tribes, who put down their weapon to run in peace in Kapenguria, Kenya. Loroupe said the motivation for the race was to use her fame to help bring about greater harmony.
In 2006, the Secretary of the United Nations, Kofe Annan, named her the United Nations Peace Ambassador, together with Roger Federer, in the United Nations Year of Sport.
She is also a member of the ‘Champions for Peace’ a group of athletes seeking to use the power of sport to bring about peace. Loroupe has also sought to advance the opportunities of Kenyan women. She is a role model and has helped many women widen their horizons and enter new fields in peace-making, education, and sports.

## Tegla Loroupe Career Timeline
Loroupe was born on May 9, 1973 in Kenya’s West Pokot region.
She emerged as a competitive runner in her youth and represented Kenya in international cross-country competition before becoming a major 10,000m athlete.
She competed at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics.
In 1993, she finished fourth in the World Championships 10,000 metres.
In 1994, she won the New York City Marathon on her debut, becoming the first African woman to win a major marathon.
Shop Walking Shoes
She defended the New York title in 1995 and won 10,000m bronze at the World Championships that year.
She finished sixth in the 10,000m at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.
Loroupe won three consecutive World Half Marathon titles from 1997 through 1999.
In 1998, she set a new marathon world best of 2:20:47 in Rotterdam.
Later that year, she set a world record in the one-hour race.
In 1999, Loroupe won another World Championships 10,000m bronze medal in a personal-best 30:32.03.
A month later, she improved her own marathon world best to 2:20:43 in Berlin.
She finished fifth in the Sydney Olympic 10,000m final in 2000.
In 2003, she established the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.
In 2011, the IOC honoured her with its World Trophy at the Women and Sport Awards.
In 2016, she served as Chef de Mission of the first Refugee Olympic Team in Rio.
Later that year, the United Nations in Kenya named her Person of the Year.
Her Foundation continues working in peacebuilding, education, refugee sport and community resilience, while Loroupe remains its public leader.

## What Is Tegla Loroupe Doing Now?
As of August 2026, Tegla Loroupe is best described as a former elite Kenyan distance runner and active peace advocate.
She remains founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.
The organisation continues to maintain its Nairobi base and Ngong refugee-athlete training centre and has broadened its work into areas including environmental resilience and education.
Loroupe also continues appearing in international sport-for-development discussions.
The United Nations featured her in its 2025 Second World Summit for Social Development programming, where she discussed using sport to advance education and opportunity.
Get Sports Gear
Tegla Loroupe’s athletics record would have been enough to establish a major legacy.
Two New York Marathon victories.
Three World Half Marathon championships.
Two global marathon bests.
Two World Championships bronze medals.
Multiple major-city marathon victories.
And three Olympic appearances.
But the second half of her public life altered how those achievements are understood.
Loroupe did not simply use sport to escape a difficult environment.
She eventually returned to the problems associated with that environment and attempted to use sport to address them.
The same running that once carried her onto podiums became a way to bring rival communities together.
The fame built through New York, Rotterdam and Berlin became a platform for refugee athletes.
And an elite career measured in minutes and seconds became a humanitarian career measured in institutions, programmes and people.
That combination is what makes Tegla Loroupe more than a former marathon record-holder.
She is one of the clearest Kenyan examples of an athlete turning sporting influence into long-term public service.

Tegla Loroupe is a former Kenyan elite distance runner, former marathon world-best holder and founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

# Loroupe breaks marathon world best in Berlin
[![Image 49: Facebook](https://www.worldathletics.org/static/facebook-white.png)](https://www.facebook.com/share.php?u=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/report/loroupe-does-it-again&title=Loroupe%20breaks%20marathon%20world%20best%20in%20Berlin "Share on Facebook")[![Image 50: Twitter](https://www.worldathletics.org/static/twitter-white.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/report/loroupe-does-it-again&text=loroupe-breaks-marathon-world-best-in-berlin "Share on X")[![Image 51: Email](https://www.worldathletics.org/static/email-white.png)](mailto:?subject=Loroupe%20breaks%20marathon%20world%20best%20in%20Berlin&body=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/report/loroupe-does-it-again "Share via email")
Kenyan distance runner Tegla Loroupe (© Getty Images)
Kenya's Tegla Loroupe improved her own world women's best time by four seconds to win the Berlin marathon in 2:20:43 before more than a million cheering spectators on Sunday.
Kenyan Josephat Kiprono won the men's race in 2:06:45, the third best time ever, leading a record field of 28,000 participants through the German capital city under near-ideal weather conditions - 15 degrees, cloudy and little wind.
The flat and fast course that wends its way through nine of the Berlin's 23 districts now holds the world's best marks for men and women: Brazilian Ronaldo da Costa won last year's race in 2:06.05.
The diminutive Loroupe, who is based in Germany, beat the previous best time of 2:20:47 for the 42.195 km race, which she set when she won the Rotterdam marathon in April 1998.

# Loroupe breaks marathon world best in Berlin
"This was my best race ever," said Loroupe, who did not realise she had set the new best mark until several minutes after crossing the finish line. "It makes it all the nicer that I did it in Germany."
Loroupe, who came in third in the 10,000 metre event at the World Championships in Seville last month, collected 180,000 marks ($96,000) for setting the world best time on top of her first-place prize of 50,000 marks ($27,000).
Loroupe had been aiming to become the first women to run faster than 2:20, but the 26-year-old slipped behind the world-best pace midway through the race as it moved through the districts of Kreuzberg and Neukoelln.
She found a new burst of energy at the 28-km (17-mile) mark in the leafy district of Steglitz and raced up the course's only significant incline, a climb of about 30 metres between the 30 and 32-km marks, to put herself back on track for the world best time.
"I hadn't expected it for a while because I had felt very tired," said Loroupe, who has lived and trained in the German town of Detmold for the last seven years. "I tried for the 2:19 mark but I didn't manage it.
"Thanks to the support of the crowd I was able to pick up the pace again," added the Kenyan, who stands 1.53 metres tall and weighs 40 kg.
"Tegla really broke the record in the last 100 metres," said her coach Volker Wagner. "I don’t think even Carl Lewis could have beaten her over the last couple of kilometres. She really sprinted right at the end."
Marleen Renders of Belgium was second in the women's race finishing in 2:23.58, followed by Russia's Svetlana Zakharova in 2:27.07.
Kiprono completed a fine day for Kenya and came close to setting a men's best time with a strong kick on the final mile of the race down the fashionable Kudamm shopping boulevard.

# Loroupe breaks marathon world best in Berlin
Only da Costa's world best mark in Berlin last year and South Africa's Gerd Thys, who set the year's best time in 2:06:32 in February in Tokyo, have been faster.
Kiprono, who came in second in the 1997 race, was followed to the line by Takayuki Inubushi of Japan in 2:06.57 and compatriot Samson Kandie in 2:08.34.
The 28,000 participants in 26th annual Berlin marathon included 4,000 rollerbladers, wheelchair racers and power walkers.
Only the New York and London marathons, with about 30,000 participants, are larger, organisers said.
